newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden lowers forecast for 1997 borrowing need.
newsitem.headline: Sweden lowers forecast for 1997 borrowing need.

text.p: Sweden's state borrowing requirement for January 1997 was expected to be zero compared to 18 billion in January 1996, the National Debt Office said on Tuesday.
The office also lowered its forecast for the 1997 borrowing requirement to 20 to 30 billion crowns from a previous forecast of 25 to 35 billion crown.

"Interest on the government debt is expected to be significantly lower in January 1997 as a result of lower coupon payments on loans 1020 and 1028, as these loans have been partly redeemed," the office said in a statement.
"Lower disbursements are also foreseen for a number of public authorities."
The office said the reason for lowering its 1997 forecast was "partly the National Economic Research Institute's brighter economic forecast."
The state's borrowing requirement for the 12-month period up to the end of November 1996 amounted to 22.8 billion crowns.
A borrowing requirement for December was forecast at 12.3 billion crowns which was 2.8 billion higher than in the previous forecast.
"The higher borrowing requirement is partly due to higher-than-forecast payments to the EU," the office said.
The borrowing need for calendar 1996 was estimated at 26 billion crowns, which was unchanged from the previous forecast.
The office said it was reducing the number of treasury bill loans from 12 to eight and concentrating volumes of bills maturing on the so-called IMM dates (in March, June, September and December).
"Over the last few years, the National Debt Office has consolidated the government debt with the aim of keeping down the gross borrowing requirement," the debt office said.
"This consolidation has been achieved by reducing the proportion of short-term loans, i.e. treasury bills.
"The rapidly falling borrowing requirement over the last few years has underpinned this change."
